checkpoints: An account owns 3 trust lines and 2 open offers: write the formula for its total reserve requirement.
Why can an account never spend its base reserve, and what attack does that prevent?
A transaction with sequence 5 lands while the account is at sequence 7: accepted or rejected, and why?
keyConcepts: Accounts are key pairs (secp256k1 or ed25519); the classic address is a base58check encoding of the account ID.
AccountRoot ledger object stores balance, sequence number, and owned-object count.
Base reserve: minimum XRP every account must hold; owner reserve: additional XRP per owned ledger entry.
Sequence numbers increment by exactly one per applied transaction; gaps or replays are rejected.
Regular keys and signer lists enable delegated and multi-party authorization.
Drops: 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops, the integer unit fees are quoted in.
labs: Generate an ed25519 and a secp256k1 wallet offline in xrpl.js and compare the resulting classic addresses.
Query account_info on Testnet for a fresh faucet account; record Balance, Sequence, and OwnerCount.
Create one trust line and one offer, then re-query OwnerCount and recompute the account's reserve lockup.
Submit two transactions with the same sequence number; confirm the second fails as a duplicate.
Assign a regular key to a test account and submit a transaction signed only with that key.
objectives: Explain how an XRPL account is defined by its key pair and address.
Compute the total reserve requirement for an account owning N ledger objects.
Predict when a transaction is rejected for a stale or duplicate sequence number.
Distinguish base reserve from owner reserve and their purpose against spam.
modules.title: Ledger Model: Accounts, Keys, Reserves, Sequences

checkpoints: What is the difference between a tec-class and a ter-class result for fee accounting?
When does multi-signing beat a regular key for operational security?
Your transaction has not appeared after 10 ledgers: is LastLedgerSequence or the queue the first thing to check?
keyConcepts: Every transaction declares type, Account, Sequence (or TicketSequence), Fee, and LastLedgerSequence.
Signing happens client-side over the canonical binary serialization; the network never sees private keys.
Multi-signing combines weighted signer-list signatures instead of one master-key signature.
Pending transactions sit in each server's transaction queue until consensus validates them.
Ledgers close roughly every 3–5 seconds via the XRPL consensus process and a supermajority of validators.
Transaction results: tesSUCCESS applied; tec/tem/ter classes distinguish claimed-cost failures, malformed, and retryable outcomes.
labs: Build, sign, and submit a Payment in xrpl.js with autofill; log the full signed blob fields.
Submit an identical transaction with a LastLedgerSequence 4 ledgers out; verify it expires unapplied.
Create a signer list on a test account and submit a multi-signed Payment with two signer signatures.
Mint 3 tickets with TicketCreate and use TicketSequence to submit 3 Payments out of order.
Subscribe to the ledger stream and measure the close interval across 20 ledgers.
objectives: Describe the lifecycle of a transaction from signing to validated ledger inclusion.
Choose between single signature, regular key, and multi-signing for a given authorization need.
Set fees and LastLedgerSequence correctly to bound a transaction's retry window.
Use ticket batching to submit sequence-independent transactions in parallel.
modules.title: Transactions, Signing, and Ledger Close

checkpoints: Why does a passive offer protect a market maker from being picked off?
A payment delivered less than Amount with no error: which flag was set and what must the recipient check?
Contrast consuming liquidity via OfferCreate versus via a path payment for a large size.
keyConcepts: Order books exist per currency-pair; offers are first-class ledger objects, not off-chain intents.
Offers match at quality (exchange rate); tfPassive offers never consume existing offers at a worse rate.
Autobridging routes currency-to-currency trades through XRP order books automatically.
Pathfinding searches trust-line and order-book graphs; Payment paths can combine both.
Partial payments (tfPartialPayment) may deliver less than the requested amount; always check delivered_amount.
Offer expiration and owner reserves make stale-order cleanup an economic design feature.
labs: Post a buy and a sell offer for a Testnet IOU/XRP pair; inspect both with book_offers.
Place a tfFillOrKill offer sized larger than book depth and confirm it either fills fully or dies.
Run path_find between two IOU-issuing test accounts and trace the chosen route hop by hop.
Execute a cross-currency Payment with SendMax and verify delivered_amount versus Amount.
Cancel all open offers via account_offers enumeration and confirm the reserve unlock.
objectives: Place and cancel limit offers with OfferCreate and OfferCancel.
Read an order book with book_offers and interpret price, quality, and depth.
Execute a cross-currency payment using ripple_path_find and explain autobridging through XRP.
Set offer flags (tfSell, tfPassive, tfFillOrKill, tfImmediateOrCancel) to control execution behavior.
modules.title: The Native DEX: Order Books, Offers, Pathfinding

checkpoints: What happens to existing holder balances when an issuer enables global freeze?
Why would a gateway set NoRipple by default on customer trust lines?
An issuer wants KYC-gated distribution: which account flag and which trust-line flow implement it?
keyConcepts: IOUs exist only where a trust line authorizes a holder to carry an issuer's currency up to a limit.
Trust lines are bilateral ledger objects; limits and quality are set independently per side.
Rippling lets a payment pass through an account's trust lines; NoRipple flags block it.
Issuers can freeze individual trust lines (tfSetFreeze) or enable account-wide freeze (lsfGlobalFreeze).
Authorized trust lines (lsfRequireAuth) let issuers approve holders before balances can be received.
The clawback feature allows issuers to reclaim issued tokens under defined conditions.
labs: Create two test accounts; set a trust line from one to an issuer account and issue 100 units.
Toggle NoRipple on the holder's trust line and attempt a rippling payment through it.
Freeze the trust line as the issuer and confirm sends fail while the freeze is active.
Enable RequireAuth on a fresh issuer and walk a new holder through the authorization handshake.
Inspect the trust line object via ledger_entry and map each field to its on-ledger meaning.
objectives: Open a trust line with TrustSet and explain limit, quality, and rippling settings.
Issue an IOU and walk through the issuer/holder balance-sheet relationship.
Apply freeze settings at the trust-line and issuer-account level and predict their effects.
Configure NoRipple flags to control whether balances can transit through an account.
modules.title: Issued Currencies: Trust Lines, Issuing, Freezing

checkpoints: A buyer wants to pay in an IOU: which mint flag must be set, and what must the seller hold?
How does brokered mode divide proceeds between seller and broker?
Why is the transfer fee immutable after minting, and who benefits from that guarantee?
keyConcepts: XLS-20 defines the on-ledger non-fungible token standard and its transaction types.
NFTokenMint takes a taxon (issuer-defined grouping/series identifier) and an optional URI.
Transfer fees are set at mint time in basis points up to the protocol maximum and flow to the issuer on secondary sales.
Flags: tfTransferable, tfBurnable, tfOnlyXRP, tfTrustLine control resale, burning, and accepted payment assets.
NFTokenCreateOffer creates buy or sell offers; tfSellOffer marks the direction; brokered mode splits proceeds.
NFTokenAcceptOffer settles a trade; NFTokenCancelOffer and NFTokenBurn complete the lifecycle.
labs: Mint a transferable NFT with a taxon and URI on Testnet; read it back via account_nfts.
List it with a sell offer denominated in XRP, then accept that offer from a second account.
Execute a brokered sale where a third account brokers between seller and buyer offers.
Mint an NFT with a transfer fee and measure the fee split on a secondary sale.
Burn an unwanted test NFT and confirm the owner's NFToken count decrements.
objectives: Mint an NFToken with NFTokenMint and explain taxon, URI, and flag choices.
Set and reason about transfer fees within the protocol's allowed range.
Trade an NFT using buy and sell NFTokenOffers, including brokered mode.
Burn an NFT and verify its removal from the owner's directory.
modules.title: XLS-20 NFTs: Minting, Taxon, Transfer Fees

checkpoints: Why must the initial AMMCreate deposit both assets in the pool's current price ratio?
A large swap moves the price: which invariant determines the new reserves?
When is holding the auction slot profitable, and what does the pool gain from auctioning it?
keyConcepts: XLS-30 defines automated market maker pools as on-ledger accounts governed by the AMM engine.
Pools hold exactly two assets and price trades against a constant-product (geometric mean) invariant.
Liquidity providers receive LP tokens proportional to their share; LP tokens are themselves ledger assets.
Single-asset deposits and withdrawals are supported, with slippage handled by the pool math.
A trading fee (capped by protocol) accrues to LPs on every swap.
The auction slot lets one account bid for discounted trading fees for a fixed number of ledgers.
labs: Create an XRP/IOU pool on Testnet with AMMCreate from a funded test account.
Deposit additional liquidity and record the LP tokens credited versus pool share.
Execute a swap into the pool and compare executed price against the pre-trade spot price.
Withdraw half your LP position as a single-asset withdrawal and verify the assets received.
Bid on the auction slot with AMMBid and observe the discounted-fee window on subsequent swaps.
objectives: Create an AMM pool with AMMCreate and explain the two-asset deposit requirement.
Deposit and withdraw liquidity, including single-asset operations and LP token accounting.
Compute a trade's price impact from the constant-product invariant.
Describe the auction slot mechanism and who benefits from holding it.
modules.title: XLS-30 AMM: Pools, LP Tokens, Auction Slot

checkpoints: What fields must you never let a library autofill blindly in a production signing service?
Your submitAndWait throws on expiration: list the three recovery steps in order.
When is a WebSocket subscription preferable to polling account_tx?
keyConcepts: xrpl.js (Node.js) and xrpl-py (Python) are the official client libraries maintained under XRPLF.
Client connects to wss endpoints; public clusters exist for mainnet, testnet, and devnet.
autofill populates Fee, Sequence, and LastLedgerSequence; sign applies the wallet's key.
submitAndWait blocks until the transaction appears in a validated ledger or expires.
Request/response methods (account_info, account_tx, tx) cover history and state reads.
Subscriptions push ledger closes and account transactions without polling.
labs: Write an xrpl.js script that connects, funds via faucet, sends 10 XRP, and disconnects cleanly.
Port the same flow to xrpl-py and compare the transaction-construction APIs.
Subscribe to the transactions stream filtered to your test account and log incoming payments live.
Implement a retry wrapper that resubmits on terQUEUED with exponential backoff.
Build a small CLI that prints any account's XRP balance, trust lines, and open offers.
objectives: Connect to a public cluster over WebSocket and manage connection lifecycle.
Construct, autofill, sign, and submit transactions with submitAndWait.
Subscribe to ledger and transaction streams for real-time application updates.
Handle common API errors and implement retry logic for ter-class results.
modules.title: Client Development with xrpl.js and xrpl-py

checkpoints: Your test account suddenly has zero balance and no history: what happened and what is the recovery?
A reporting-mode node versus a stock server: which serves your exchange's order-book API?
Name three concrete separations between your test and mainnet workflows.
keyConcepts: Testnet and Devnet are parallel networks with worthless XRP dispensed by public faucets.
Faucets fund new test accounts; test networks reset periodically, wiping state.
Never reuse test seeds or test patterns with real funds; keep environments strictly separated.
rippled can run as a validator, a stock server, or in reporting mode for heavy API workloads.
History modes range from full history to online-delete with configurable retention.
Public API clusters are rate-limited and shared; production apps typically run dedicated infrastructure.
labs: Fund two accounts from the faucet and run a full issue-trust-pay-settle cycle entirely on Testnet.
Point the same script at Devnet and note endpoint and network differences.
Simulate a testnet reset: document which artifacts of your workflow survive and which must be rebuilt.
Draft a rippled config choosing a history mode for a read-heavy analytics use case, with justification.
Load-test your script against the public Testnet cluster and record where rate limits bite.
objectives: Stand up a safe test loop using faucets and funded Testnet/Devnet accounts.
Distinguish testnet, devnet, and mainnet endpoints and their reset behaviors.
Describe rippled operating modes and when each fits (full history vs. current ledger).
Choose an API access strategy: public cluster, reporting mode, or self-hosted node.
modules.title: Testnet Workflow and Node Operations
